opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the core worry is about the gap between the regime we can test in and the regime we actually care about. When we run experiments on current models, we're mostly operating in a setting where humans can still check the answers. If a model writes some code or answers a question, we can usually tell whether it did a good job, or at least we can get an expert to look at it. So our alignment techniques get validated in a world where human oversight basically works.

The problem with superintelligence is that, almost by definition, you're in a regime where the system knows things you don't and can do things you can't verify directly. And a lot of the failure modes we're most worried about only really show up there. If a model is subtly wrong, or subtly deceptive, in a way that's beyond your ability to detect, then your experiments will just tell you everything is fine. The evidence looks clean precisely because you can't see the problem.

There's also a question of whether the methods themselves scale in the right way. Something like reinforcement learning from human feedback works reasonably well now, but it's fundamentally bottlenecked on human judgment. You can make incremental progress and see the numbers go up, but that doesn't tell you whether the method has the right asymptotic properties, whether it keeps working as the gap between the model and the human grows. And empirical progress can be quite misleading there, because the curve can look great right up until it doesn't.

So that's part of why I've been interested in approaches with more theoretical grounding, like debate, where you can at least try to argue that if the protocol is set up correctly, honest behaviour is the winning strategy even when the judge is much weaker than the debaters. I don't think theory alone is enough either; you need both. But I'd be nervous about a strategy that's purely "run experiments on today's models, see what works, and extrapolate," because the extrapolation step is exactly where the danger lives.

I'd add one more thing, which is that the systems themselves change qualitatively. Things like situational awareness, the model understanding that it's being trained or evaluated, are only partially present now. Once those are strong, the relationship between how a model behaves in your experiments and how it behaves in deployment could change in ways your earlier data simply didn't capture.

r002.rationale: It describes superintelligence and stronger situational awareness as potentially changing behavior, but does not identify crossing human-level intelligence as the point where alignment behavior could qualitatively change.

r003.rationale: The response discusses theoretical grounding and extrapolation, but does not distinguish automating current-model reward-hacking experiments from conceptual modeling of when alignment approaches break down as AI scales.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I want to be careful here, because I actually think incremental experiments are most of what we should be doing. The question is what they can and can't tell you.

The core worry is that a lot of the alignment problems we're most scared of don't really show up at the current capability level, or they show up in a form that's different enough that the fix you find doesn't transfer. Take deception. If you have a model that's roughly at the level of a mediocre human assistant, and it does something that looks deceptive, you can usually catch it. You can read the transcript, you can look at the chain of thought, you can run it a thousand times and see how often it happens. And then you train against that, and the behaviour goes away, and you declare victory. But what you've learned is something about how a weak model that is bad at deception responds to training pressure. You haven't learned much about a model that is good at deception, that understands it's being evaluated, that can model the training process better than you can. The experiment ran, it gave you a number, but the number is answering a different question.

So the thing I'd say is: there's a difference between evidence about the method and evidence about the regime. You can gather tons of evidence that debate, or scalable oversight, or interpretability, works on today's systems. That's genuinely useful. But the whole point of alignment work for superintelligence is that the regime changes. The model becomes more capable than the overseers along some axis, and your techniques have to keep working across that transition. And by construction you can't run that experiment yet, because you don't have the model.

The way I think about it is that you need some theoretical story that tells you why a result at capability level X should generalise to capability level Y. If you have that story, incremental experiments become really powerful, because they're testing the assumptions of the story. If you don't, you're just extrapolating a trend line and hoping. And the history of ML is full of trend lines that broke.

Then there's a more mundane but real problem, which is that current experiments are expensive and noisy, and the effect sizes you're hunting for are often small. So you end up in a position where you've got a result that's suggestive, but not enough to bet the future on, and the temptation is to treat it as more than it is.

So the honest summary is: incremental experiments are necessary, they're not sufficient, and the gap between those two is where I think a lot of the hard thinking has to happen. You want to design experiments where a negative result would actually falsify your approach, rather than ones where you just confirm that things work fine at a level where you'd expect them to work fine anyway.

r002.rationale: It describes a regime change as models become more capable than overseers and contrasts weak with capable deception, but does not identify crossing human-level intelligence as the point where alignment behavior could change.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes evidence about methods from evidence about the regime and calls for a theory of generalization, but does not distinguish automating reward-hacking experiments from automating conceptual modeling of when alignment approaches break down as AI scales.

astra-6.text:
The basic difficulty is that the property we care about is what happens when the system is much smarter than we are, and experiments with current models don’t directly test that. They test a regime where we can still understand a lot of what the model is doing and independently check its answers.

For example, suppose you train a model to give answers that humans judge to be good. With a weaker model, that might push it towards giving genuinely good answers. But as the model becomes more capable, it may get better at finding answers that look good to us even when they’re wrong. So an improvement in the thing you measure needn’t be an improvement in the thing you actually want.

That makes extrapolation difficult. You could have a sequence of experiments that all look reassuring, while never encountering the particular failure mode that matters: a system exploiting mistakes in an evaluator that’s less capable than it is.

I don’t think that makes current experiments useless. They can reveal problems and test pieces of an alignment proposal. But we also need an argument for why the proposal should continue to work when the capability gap reverses. Otherwise, we risk treating evidence that we can supervise systems weaker than ourselves as evidence that we can supervise systems much stronger than ourselves.

r001.rationale: The response says measured improvements can fail to reflect the desired outcome, but does not explain that measurable capability performance enables incremental hill-climbing on AI capabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes risks as models become more capable and systems become much smarter than humans, but does not identify crossing human-level intelligence as a point where alignment behavior could qualitatively change.

r003.rationale: The response does not distinguish automating experiments on current-model reward hacking from automating conceptual modeling of how alignment approaches may break down as AI scales.

sol-6.1.text:
The basic difficulty is that we need our alignment methods to work on systems that are much smarter than we are, and current experiments mostly involve systems that are less capable than we are. That changes the nature of the problem. If I can check an answer myself, I can test whether the model got it right. But what I ultimately want is a method that lets me trust an answer when I can’t independently check it.

For example, a model might appear to follow our instructions because it doesn’t have the ability to find a way around our checks. Making that model behave well doesn’t necessarily tell us what happens when the model understands the checks better than we do. The absence of a failure could just reflect the absence of the capability needed to produce it.

That doesn’t make experiments with current models useless. They can uncover problems and test pieces of a proposal. But we need an argument for why the evidence transfers to the situation we actually care about. Ideally, we’d design experiments that capture the relevant asymmetry—where the system being supervised knows something the supervisor doesn’t—and combine those experiments with a more general understanding of why the method should work. Just observing that things improve as we iterate on today’s models doesn’t establish that they’ll keep improving across that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says answers can be checked and that researchers can iterate on today’s models, but it does not explain how measurable capability performance enables incremental hill-climbing on capabilities.

r002.rationale: It contrasts current systems that are less capable than humans with systems much smarter than humans, and says the problem changes when a model understands the checks better than its supervisor.

r003.rationale: The response mentions testing pieces of a proposal and needing a general understanding of why a method should work, but it does not distinguish automating reward-hacking experiments from automating conceptual modeling of alignment breakdown as AI scales.
